title: Grade 12 daily reading
overview: A year of authentic poems, fiction, drama and philosophical essays develops patient rereading, sustained attention and independent judgment. Complete short works alternate with clearly bounded continuous excerpts from longer works. Read aloud difficult sentences or verse, reconstruct the speaker’s claim, and use the supplied evidence to test more than one defensible interpretation. Suggested 25–30 minute budgets include rereading and discussion; actual pace varies. Historical religious, political and social assumptions are identified in context without rewriting the originals.

progression.rationale: Reread ten complete Hopkins poems, tracing how syntax, sound and images develop religious and psychological claims. Build the habit of distinguishing a speaker’s assertion from its figurative support.
Read seven complete Joyce stories across fifteen nights, holding details across continuations and separating restricted perspectives from what the narrative establishes.
Compare ten Yeats poems that turn revolution, historical change, prayer and personal memory into deliberately unsettled lyric arguments. Test what the images invite without reducing them to slogans.
Read ten complete Donne poems, following their surprising analogies and changes of address. Identify where persuasive ingenuity clarifies a relationship and where it becomes an assertion to question.

Read The Dead continuously and completely over ten nights. Carry early judgments forward and revise them as Gabriel’s public performance gives way to Gretta’s distinct memory and a transformed final perspective.

progression.focus: Epic rhetoric and the framing narrator
progression.rationale: Read all of Paradise Lost Book I in five continuous portions. Distinguish Satan’s appeals to freedom and courage from the narrator’s larger framing, while managing extended syntax and allusions.
Follow ten substantial passages from Plato’s Republic VI–VII in Jowett’s translation. Trace the purpose and limits of analogies before evaluating the responsibilities they assign to educated people.

progression.focus: Liberty, disagreement and the limits of power
progression.rationale: Read Mill’s connected arguments across fifteen chosen passages. Reconstruct distinctions, reasons, objections and boundary cases; assess a claim in its argumentative setting rather than as an isolated maxim.

progression.focus: Education and equality as institutional questions
progression.rationale: Read fifteen substantial Wollstonecraft selections. Examine how social arrangements shape capacities, distinguish a criticism of training from a claim about nature, and evaluate the evidence and assumptions of her reform proposals.

Work through fifteen Russell selections with increasing independence. Distinguish objects, appearances, knowledge and inference, reconstructing why each distinction matters and where certainty remains limited.

progression.focus: Testing persuasion in an epic temptation
progression.rationale: Return to Milton through five Book IX excerpts. Apply the year’s work on premises, desire and rhetorical pressure to the temptation and its consequences, preserving the difference between attractive speech and warranted conclusion.

Follow fifteen substantial Heart of Darkness excerpts from the framing river to the final encounter and return. Track embedded voices, racial language, material exploitation and what Marlow’s judgments can and cannot establish.

Read consecutive chapters I–X of The Turn of the Screw. Keep a record of observation, inference and retrospective narration; allow later details to complicate explanations without prematurely settling the apparitions’ nature.

Read ten A Room of One’s Own excerpts. Evaluate Woolf’s mixtures of fictional experiment, documentary claim, satire and institutional argument while connecting access to resources with possibilities for authorship.

Read Murray’s complete Oedipus King of Thebes in ten continuous parts. Track the gap between what characters intend, know and discover; examine competing testimony and the chorus’s changing judgments.

progression.focus: Independent judgment across a dramatic sequence
progression.rationale: Read fifteen connected Hamlet selections through the conclusion, with omitted action identified in context. Integrate public language, private speech, staged evidence and uncertain motives; test claims about responsibility and the final surviving story.

days.title: God’s Grandeur
days.challenge: Untangle compressed comparisons and the sonnet’s argumentative turn.
days.focus: Industrial damage and the grounds for renewed hope.
days.context: Read twice aloud. Hopkins moves from the world’s divine charge through human damage to a final explanation of renewal.

excerpt.locator: God's Grandeur; complete individual work; opens “THE world is charged with the grandeur of God. It will flame out, like shining from shook foil; It g”; closes “ings-- Because the Holy Ghost over the bent World broods with warm breast and with ah! bright wings.”.

questions.prompt: What different accounts of divine energy do shaken foil and crushed oil offer?
facilitatorNotes: Foil suggests sudden reflected brilliance; pressed oil suggests concentrated release. Both make invisible grandeur perceptible, but neither requires an undamaged landscape.
evidence: like shining from shook foil

questions.prompt: How do repeated words and bodily sensations make the criticism of trade concrete?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated treading accumulates pressure; smudge, smell and shoes register contamination and loss of direct contact. Discuss the sonic insistence of the repeated have trod.
evidence: Generations have trod, have trod, have trod;

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza deny the damage described earlier? Explain the work of its opening concession.
facilitatorNotes: And for all this concedes damage while claiming a deeper freshness. The brooding bird offers protective renewal, not evidence that human damage never occurred.
evidence: And for all this, nature is never spent;

days.title: The Starlight Night
days.challenge: Follow rapid shifts among urban, mineral, agricultural and sacred images.
days.focus: Vision as invitation, purchase and threshold.
days.context: Notice the imperatives: the poem first teaches its listener to look and then changes what looking demands.

excerpt.locator: The Starlight Night; complete individual work; opens “LOOK at the stars! look, look up at the skies! O look at all the fire-folk sitting in the air! The b”; closes “s. This piece-bright paling shuts the spouse Christ home, Christ and his mother and all his hallows.”.

questions.prompt: Why describe stars as boroughs and citadels rather than merely points of light?
facilitatorNotes: These images make the sky inhabited and organized; the later sacred household extends that impression. Other readings may emphasize distance or defensive walls.
evidence: The bright boroughs, the circle-citadels there!

questions.prompt: What surprise follows the command to buy, and how does it redefine the earlier prize?
facilitatorNotes: The price is prayer, patience, alms and vows rather than money. The language of acquisition becomes spiritual discipline and generosity.
evidence: Prayer, patience, alms,

questions.prompt: Does the final paling give access or mark separation? Defend a reading using the barn and household images.
facilitatorNotes: A paling can enclose and reveal: glittering visible creation forms a boundary around sacred presence. Both invitation and limitation fit the imagery; explain their relation.
evidence: This piece-bright paling shuts the spouse

days.title: Spring
days.challenge: Connect sensory abundance to a plea whose syntax is interrupted and urgent.
days.focus: How a description of spring becomes an argument about innocence.
days.context: The opening celebrates a season; the second stanza addresses Christ. Follow the changing audience.

excerpt.locator: Spring; complete individual work; opens “NOTHING is so beautiful as spring-- When weeds, in wheels, shoot long and lovely and lush; Thrush's ”; closes “, Innocent mind and Mayday in girl and boy, Most, O maid's child, thy choice and worthy the winning.”.

questions.prompt: How do rinse, wring and lightnings make birdsong more than a pleasant background?
facilitatorNotes: The verbs give sound cleansing pressure and a sudden physical impact. The ear is acted upon, so the experience is startling rather than passive.
evidence: does so rinse and wring

questions.prompt: What does the question about juice and joy ask the reader to reconsider?
facilitatorNotes: It turns the catalogue of sensations toward their origin and meaning, interpreting present growth as a remnant of Eden. The poem moves from observation to theological inference.
evidence: What is all this juice and all this joy?

questions.prompt: Why does the prayer repeat before, and what changes between the first and last lines?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker fears beauty and innocence may sour; urgency replaces the opening confident superlative. The prayer asks for preservation rather than proving spring itself can prevent loss.
evidence: Before it cloud, Christ, lord, and sour with sinning,

days.title: The Lantern out of Doors
days.challenge: Track an extended analogy while identifying its stated limit.
days.focus: Human attention contrasted with enduring care.
days.context: A moving light prompts speculation about strangers. The poem later admits a failure of the observer’s own attention.

excerpt.locator: The Lantern out of Doors; complete individual work; opens “SOMETIMES a lantern moves along the night, That interests our eyes. And who goes there? I think; whe”; closes “art wánts, care haúnts, foot fóllows kínd, Their ránsom, théir rescue, ánd first, fást, last friénd.”.

questions.prompt: How does wading make the lantern’s movement through darkness feel?
facilitatorNotes: Darkness becomes a resistant medium; the person seems vulnerable and laboring. The small moving light also creates curiosity about a life beyond the observer’s knowledge.
evidence: his wading light

questions.prompt: Where does the speaker admit that curiosity is insufficient?
facilitatorNotes: He cannot follow a person to the end and admits that absence becomes forgetfulness. This confession prevents the opening interest from appearing equivalent to sustained care.
evidence: out of sight is out of mind

questions.prompt: How does the final sequence of verbs change the kind of attention being described?
facilitatorNotes: Seeing becomes wanting, caring, following, ransoming and rescuing. Christ’s care is active and continuous; readers can analyze that claim without sharing its theology.
evidence: Their ránsom, théir rescue, ánd first, fást, last friénd.

days.title: The Sea and the Skylark
days.challenge: Hear competing sound patterns and test the logic of the poem’s moral comparison.
days.focus: Natural recurrence and a judgment on human progress.
days.context: Read the sea and lark passages aloud before considering the turn toward the town.

excerpt.locator: The Sea and the Skylark; complete individual work; opens “ON ear and ear two noises too old to end Trench--right, the tide that ramps against the shore; With ”; closes “ make and making break, are breaking, down To man's last dust, drain fast towards man's first slime.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening place the reader between sea and skylark?
facilitatorNotes: Right and left locate separate sound sources, while the two ears receive both. The reader occupies the listening body rather than a distant panoramic viewpoint.
evidence: ON ear and ear two noises too old to end

questions.prompt: Why is the lark’s music compared to a skein and a winch?
facilitatorNotes: Unwinding thread and rotating machinery suggest repeated, intricately produced sound. The language borrows human craft to praise nature, complicating the later rejection of human making.
evidence: His rash-fresh re-winded new-skeinèd score

questions.prompt: What tension appears when life’s crown becomes first slime?
facilitatorNotes: Human exceptionalism is invoked and overturned. The final decline may be read as moral decay rather than a literal biological theory; the imagery supports that distinction.
evidence: To man's last dust, drain fast towards man's first slime.

days.title: Pied Beauty
days.challenge: Explain how a very short catalogue builds a claim through unlike examples.
days.focus: Variation, labor and unchanging beauty.
days.context: The shortened sonnet includes natural marks, worked land and trades. Reread the final two lines against that variety.

excerpt.locator: Pied Beauty; complete individual work; opens “GLORY be to God for dappled things-- For skies of couple-colour as a brinded cow; For rose-moles all”; closes “th swift, slow; sweet, sour; adazzle, dim; He fathers-forth whose beauty is past change: Praise him.”.

questions.prompt: What connects cow, sky, trout and chestnuts without making them identical?
facilitatorNotes: Contrasting color and patterned surfaces connect them. The surprising comparisons preserve each object’s distinctiveness while gathering them under dappled beauty.
evidence: For skies of couple-colour as a brinded cow;

questions.prompt: Why include trades and their equipment beside natural objects?
facilitatorNotes: Human making joins the catalogue of particular forms. This praise complicates any assumption that Hopkins values only untouched nature.
evidence: And áll trádes, their gear and tackle and trim.

questions.prompt: How can changeable things praise a beauty said to be past change?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker distinguishes varied manifestations from their constant divine source. Alternatively discuss the unresolved conceptual leap: the catalogue invites that belief but does not logically prove it.
evidence: He fathers-forth whose beauty is past change:

days.title: The Caged Skylark
days.challenge: Distinguish the terms of a sustained analogy from the qualification that revises it.
days.focus: Embodiment, confinement and freedom.
days.context: The bird and human spirit appear parallel at first. Watch how the sestet resists a simple body-bad/spirit-good reading.

excerpt.locator: The Caged Skylark; complete individual work; opens “As a dare-gale skylark scanted in a dull cage Man's mounting spirit in his bone-house, mean house, d”; closes “, But uncumbered: meadow-down is not distressed For a rainbow footing it nor he for his bónes rísen.”.

questions.prompt: What does the pairing of bone-house and mean house suggest about ordinary embodiment?
facilitatorNotes: The body seems cramped and humble, like a cage that limits a naturally mounting spirit. The word house also leaves open the possibility of shelter.
evidence: Man's mounting spirit in his bone-house, mean house,

questions.prompt: Why interrupt the comparison with the bird’s need for rest?
facilitatorNotes: The bird needs a home; freedom does not mean endless flight or the absence of all physical conditions. The crucial contrast becomes chosen nest versus prison.
evidence: But his own nest, wild nest, no prison.

questions.prompt: What does the rainbow image contribute to the imagined risen body?
facilitatorNotes: A rainbow touches a meadow without burdening it. The image imagines embodiment without oppressive weight, revising the opening identification of flesh with confinement.
evidence: For a rainbow footing it nor he for his bónes rísen.

days.title: Binsey Poplars
days.challenge: Follow sound and repetition while separating a local loss from a general ecological claim.
days.focus: Irreversible damage and the limits of improvement.
days.context: The subtitle records the felling of trees in 1879. Read the changes in tempo from moving shade to repeated final lament.

excerpt.locator: Binsey Poplars felled 1879; complete individual work; opens “MY aspens dear, whose airy cages quelled, Quelled or quenched in leaves the leaping sun, All felled,”; closes “s of havoc únselve The sweet especial scene, Rural scene, a rural scene, Sweet especial rural scene.”.

questions.prompt: How does the first stanza recreate the trees’ activity before recording their loss?
facilitatorNotes: Cages filter leaping sun; shadows move, swim and sink. The living pattern makes the repeated felled more than a report of removed objects.
evidence: All felled, felled, are all felled;

questions.prompt: Why compare damage to the countryside with damage to an eye?
facilitatorNotes: A small puncture can destroy a complex capacity. The analogy argues that apparent physical smallness of an intervention does not measure the scale of its loss.
evidence: But a prick will make no eye at all,

questions.prompt: What does the final repetition preserve that the felling cannot?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker repeats the scene’s sweetness and particularity, but cannot restore it or fully transmit it to later people. The verbal return enacts grief and attempts a record.
evidence: After-comers cannot guess the beauty been.

days.title: Spring and Fall: to a young child
days.challenge: Distinguish a child’s expressed grief from an adult speaker’s interpretation.
days.focus: The movement from seasonal loss to mortality.
days.context: Margaret mourns falling leaves. The adult speaker claims to understand a sorrow she cannot yet name.
days.contentNote: Meditation on grief and mortality.

excerpt.locator: Spring and Fall: to a young child; complete individual work; opens “MÁRGARÉT, áre you gríeving Over Goldengrove unleaving? Leáves, líke the things of man, you With your”; closes “What heart heard of, ghost guessed: It ís the blight man was born for, It is Margaret you mourn for.”.

questions.prompt: How does Goldengrove unleaving make the setting and event inseparable?
facilitatorNotes: The rich compound place-name and invented verb join beauty to its undoing. Sound makes the loss feel like the dismantling of the place’s identity.
evidence: Over Goldengrove unleaving?

questions.prompt: Does the speaker say adulthood cures grief?
facilitatorNotes: No: older people may react more coldly to leaves yet understand their own reason for weeping. Knowledge changes the object and expression of grief, not its source.
evidence: And yet you wíll weep and know why.

questions.prompt: What evidence supports the final claim, and what remains the speaker’s interpretation?
facilitatorNotes: Seasonal decay supplies an analogy for human death. Margaret’s actual self-understanding is not reported; the adult projects a universal explanation onto her feeling.
evidence: It is Margaret you mourn for.

days.title: Carrion Comfort
days.challenge: Reconstruct the shifting addressee and argument in a poem of spiritual crisis.
days.focus: Resistance, struggle and uncertain retrospective meaning.
days.context: The speaker first addresses Despair, then a terrifying power finally named as God. Pause at each question and change of pronoun.
days.contentNote: Intense despair and religious anguish, followed by resistance and a contested interpretation of suffering.

excerpt.locator: (Carrion Comfort); complete individual work; opens “NOT, I'll not, carrion comfort, Despair, not feast on thee; Not untwist--slack they may be--these la”; closes “t each one? That night, that year Of now done darkness I wretch lay wrestling with (my God!) my God.”.

questions.prompt: How does the opening turn an apparent inability into a minimal assertion of agency?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker refuses despair as carrion nourishment and insists on being able to hope, wish or resist. These are small capacities, not a claim that suffering has vanished.
evidence: Cán something, hope, wish day come, not choose not to be.

questions.prompt: How does the grain-and-chaff image reinterpret the earlier violent encounter?
facilitatorNotes: It suggests a purifying separation in which something valuable survives. Yet the questions and seems keep retrospective certainty unstable.
evidence: That my chaff might fly; my grain lie, sheer

questions.prompt: Why does the speaker ask which participant deserves cheering?
facilitatorNotes: The struggle joins resistance to a possible divine purpose, so victor and sufferer cannot be neatly separated. The final repeated my God carries recognition, intimacy and astonishment.
evidence: Cheer whom though?

days.title: The Sisters — part 1: words left unfinished
days.challenge: Separate observation, adult insinuation and a child’s dream.
days.focus: How withheld explanations shape a narrator’s fear and fascination.
days.context: An unnamed boy learns that Father Flynn, an older priest who taught him, has died. The story gives access to the boy’s impressions rather than an authoritative diagnosis.
days.contentNote: Death, illness and ambiguous adult insinuations about a priest’s relationship with a child; the story does not establish a specific accusation.

excerpt.locator: The Sisters; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–30; opens “There was no hope for him this time: it was the third stroke. Night after night I had passed the hou”; closes “ the customs were strange—in Persia, I thought. . . . But I could not remember the end of the dream.”.

questions.prompt: Why begin with a lighted window and the word paralysis instead of a direct announcement of death?
facilitatorNotes: The boy reads signs from outside and gives an unfamiliar word a frightening agency. The opening establishes interpretation under uncertainty.
evidence: It filled me with fear, and yet I longed to be nearer to it

questions.prompt: What can readers responsibly infer from Cotter’s unfinished sentences?
facilitatorNotes: They establish adult unease and exclusion of the child, but do not state a specific offense. Treating insinuation as a proven accusation would repeat the story’s problem of uncertain knowledge.
evidence: I puzzled my head to extract meaning from his unfinished sentences.

questions.prompt: Why is the boy disturbed by his own sensation of freedom?
facilitatorNotes: He recognizes a feeling inconsistent with expected mourning and with gratitude for instruction. That conflict suggests a burdensome relationship without fully defining its nature.
evidence: a sensation of freedom as if I had been freed from something by his death.

days.title: The Sisters — part 2: the broken chalice
days.challenge: Evaluate testimony that appears explanatory but remains incomplete.
days.focus: Ritual reassurance, material details and unresolved absence.
days.context: The boy has learned of Father Flynn’s death and felt an unsettling mixture of grief and relief. His aunt now takes him to visit the priest’s sisters.
days.contentNote: Mourning, mental distress and a deathbed visit.

excerpt.locator: The Sisters; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 31–74; opens “In the evening my aunt took me with her to visit the house of mourning. It was after sunset; but the”; closes “ourse, when they saw that, that made them think that there was something gone wrong with him. . . ."”.

questions.prompt: How does the boy’s imagined smile differ from what he actually sees at the coffin?
facilitatorNotes: He corrects his first impression: the face is solemn and truculent. This explicit revision warns readers that the narrator’s projections and observations are not interchangeable.
evidence: But no. When we rose and went up to the head of the bed I saw that he was not smiling.

questions.prompt: What do the sisters’ practical details add to the repeated claim that the death was beautiful?
facilitatorNotes: Work, expense, exhaustion and help from others anchor the ritual language in care and poverty. The conventional reassurance does not eliminate their burden or uncertainty.
evidence: All the work we had, she and me

questions.prompt: Does the broken-chalice story finally explain Father Flynn?
facilitatorNotes: It offers an account of a turning point but relies on they say and the sisters’ interpretation. The final unfinished report leaves the priest’s inner experience inaccessible.
evidence: It was that chalice he broke.

days.title: Araby — part 1: a private romance
days.challenge: Distinguish the boy’s heightened figurative world from ordinary events.
days.focus: Religious language and the making of an imagined quest.
days.context: A boy in Dublin watches a neighbor’s sister and promises to bring her something from a bazaar called Araby.

excerpt.locator: Araby; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–12; opens “North Richmond Street, being blind, was a quiet street except at the hour when the Christian Brother”; closes “now that it stood between me and my desire, seemed to me child's play, ugly monotonous child's play.”.

questions.prompt: What effect does the opening blind street have on the later promise of an enchanted elsewhere?
facilitatorNotes: The closed, watchful street contrasts with the imagined expansiveness of Araby. Its personified houses also suggest ordinary social constraint.
evidence: North Richmond Street, being blind,

questions.prompt: What does the chalice comparison reveal about the narrator’s relation to the girl?
facilitatorNotes: He turns everyday desire into a sacred mission, although he scarcely knows her. It reveals the intensity of his imagination rather than the depth of a mutual relationship.
evidence: I imagined that I bore my chalice safely through a throng of foes.

questions.prompt: How does the older narrative voice qualify the boy’s excitement?
facilitatorNotes: Follies and confused adoration introduce retrospective distance. The narrator remembers the sensation vividly while giving readers language that questions it.
evidence: What innumerable follies laid waste my waking and sleeping thoughts after that evening!

days.title: Araby — part 2: the light goes out
days.challenge: Trace an emotional reversal without reducing it to a single cause.
days.focus: The collision of private fantasy, commerce and indifference.
days.context: The boy has promised a gift and imagined the bazaar as an enchanted destination. Adult delays now threaten his journey.

excerpt.locator: Araby; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 13–37; opens “On Saturday morning I reminded my uncle that I wished to go to the bazaar in the evening. He was fus”; closes “ I saw myself as a creature driven and derided by vanity; and my eyes burned with anguish and anger.”.

questions.prompt: How do the uncle’s delay and the slow train reshape the imagined heroic errand?
facilitatorNotes: The errand depends on money, permission and transport; mundane delays diminish the boy’s agency and intensify his investment.
evidence: After an intolerable delay the train moved out of the station slowly.

questions.prompt: Why does the bazaar’s churchlike silence not fulfill the earlier sacred imagery?
facilitatorNotes: Closed stalls, money counting and indifferent salesmanship replace devotion. The resemblance is to a service already over, making the sacred comparison feel emptied out.
evidence: a silence like that which pervades a church after a service.

questions.prompt: Is the final verdict on vanity necessarily the only judgment readers can make of the boy?
facilitatorNotes: It is his intense self-judgment. Readers may also see ordinary adolescent longing and adult neglect; support an interpretation without treating his shame as the author’s final moral.
evidence: a creature driven and derided by vanity

days.title: Eveline
days.challenge: Track free indirect thought and distinguish remembered danger from imagined rescue.
days.focus: Duty, fear and the limits of a visible final gesture.
days.context: Eveline considers leaving Dublin with Frank. The narrative stays close to her thoughts while leaving the future of either choice uncertain.
days.contentNote: Domestic intimidation and grief; historical disability and ethnic language appears in the characters’ world.

excerpt.locator: Eveline; complete individual work; opens “She sat at the window watching the evening invade the avenue. Her head was leaned against the window”; closes “ him, passive, like a helpless animal. Her eyes gave him no sign of love or farewell or recognition.”.

questions.prompt: How do the two returns to dusty cretonne affect the apparent progress of Eveline’s decision?
facilitatorNotes: The repeated smell returns her to the same physical position while her mind travels through alternatives. Familiarity is comforting and oppressive at once.
evidence: inhaling the odour of dusty cretonne.

questions.prompt: What evidence complicates both the claim that home is safe and the claim that Frank will save her?
facilitatorNotes: Threatened violence and financial control undermine home’s security; Frank’s future is largely reported or imagined. Students should separate real observations from hopes without inventing criminal motives for him.
evidence: He would give her life, perhaps love, too.

questions.prompt: What changes between the wish to escape and the image of drowning?
facilitatorNotes: A proposed rescue becomes a threatening sea in her distressed perception. The final lack of recognition conveys paralysis but does not provide direct access to a settled, reasoned decision.
evidence: All the seas of the world tumbled about her heart.

days.title: Clay — part 1: preparations for an evening
days.challenge: Notice the distance between soothing narration and details that trouble it.
days.focus: Politeness, independence and suppressed disappointment.
days.context: Maria works at a laundry and plans a holiday visit to the family of a man she helped raise. Hallow Eve games traditionally used objects to predict a participant’s future.
days.contentNote: Historical institutional life, sectarian assumptions and drinking.

excerpt.locator: Clay; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–14; opens “The matron had given her leave to go out as soon as the women's tea, was over and Maria looked forwa”; closes “ head under the rain, she thought how easy it was to know a gentleman even when he has a drop taken.”.

questions.prompt: What do Maria’s exact timetable, portions and budget reveal about her place in this world?
facilitatorNotes: She is competent, careful and proud of modest independence. The precision also shows how a small expense or delay could matter greatly to her evening.
evidence: She would have five shillings clear after paying tram fare.

questions.prompt: How does disappointed shyness qualify Maria’s declaration that she wants no ring or man?
facilitatorNotes: The description introduces a feeling her polite response does not acknowledge. It invites, but does not compel, an inference of unfulfilled desire.
evidence: disappointed shyness

questions.prompt: What inconsistency appears in Maria’s judgments about drinking?
facilitatorNotes: She fears Joe’s changed behavior when drunk but excuses the courteous stranger. The distinction may show context-sensitive judgment or the influence of welcome attention.
evidence: how easy it was to know a gentleman even when he has a drop taken.

days.title: Clay — part 2: the object nobody names
days.challenge: Interpret omissions while respecting the limits of the viewpoint.
days.focus: Protective kindness, concealment and the emotional force of a repeated song.
days.context: Maria has bought cakes and accepted friendly attention on a tram. At Joe’s house, the planned surprise and the fortune-telling game do not go as expected.
days.contentNote: An implied death omen, disappointment and alcohol use.

excerpt.locator: Clay; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 15–25; opens “Everybody said: "O, here's Maria!" when she came to Joe's house. Joe was there, having come home fro”; closes “d what he was looking for and in the end he had to ask his wife to tell him where the corkscrew was.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the lost plumcake cause more distress than its small size might suggest?
facilitatorNotes: It represents money, careful planning and a special gift. Her confusion with the gentleman links an enjoyable moment to shame and disappointed generosity.
evidence: the failure of her little surprise

questions.prompt: How is the disturbing object communicated without being named in the narrative?
facilitatorNotes: Its wet texture, the garden reference, silence and hurried replacement point toward the title’s clay. The group’s reaction communicates a death omen while Maria understands only that the turn was wrong.
evidence: She felt a soft wet substance with her fingers

questions.prompt: How do the repeated first verse and the final corkscrew complicate an entirely cheerful ending?
facilitatorNotes: The song repeats desired love and grandeur while skipping its progression; Joe’s tears coexist with drinking and evasion. Kindness is real, but it does not repair every absence.
evidence: But no one tried to show her her mistake;

days.title: A Painful Case — part 1: order and intimacy
days.challenge: Analyze a self-image that the descriptive details partly undermine.
days.focus: The difference between intellectual companionship and mutual recognition.
days.context: James Duffy organizes a life of isolation. A chance meeting introduces Mrs. Sinico, whose responses do not remain within his preferred categories.
days.contentNote: An emotionally intimate relationship outside marriage and its abrupt rejection.

excerpt.locator: A Painful Case; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–13; opens “Mr. James Duffy lived in Chapelizod because he wished to live as far as possible from the city of wh”; closes “good-bye quickly and left her. A few days later he received a parcel containing his books and music.”.

questions.prompt: What does Duffy’s habit of composing sentences about himself in the third person suggest?
facilitatorNotes: He watches and narrates himself at a distance, making life an object of control. This can suggest reflective intelligence as well as emotional estrangement.
evidence: a subject in the third person and a predicate in the past tense.

questions.prompt: How reciprocal is the intellectual relationship described here?
facilitatorNotes: He lends books and provides ideas; she listens and urges growth. Warmth changes him, yet the unequal phrasing and his pleasure in his own voice raise questions about genuine mutual attention.
evidence: Sometimes he caught himself listening to the sound of his own voice.

questions.prompt: Why call their former room a ruined confessional?
facilitatorNotes: He had entrusted thoughts to her while preserving an idealized, disembodied relation. Her touch changes what he thinks the intimacy means; ruined is closely tied to his perspective.
evidence: their ruined confessional

days.title: A Painful Case — part 2: a public account
days.challenge: Distinguish a fictional inquest’s evidence, institutional interests and claims of certainty.
days.focus: How a newspaper transforms a private life into a case.
days.context: Four years after Duffy breaks off contact, a report of Mrs. Sinico’s death interrupts his routine. The newspaper passage is part of Joyce’s fiction, not an external historical document.
days.contentNote: A fatal railway accident, alcohol dependence and bereavement; the account does not establish intent.

excerpt.locator: A Painful Case; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 14–31; opens “Four years passed. Mr. Duffy returned to his even way of life. His room still bore witness of the or”; closes “measures to prevent the possibility of similar accidents in the future. No blame attached to anyone.”.

questions.prompt: How does the cold meal make Duffy’s response visible before the report is disclosed?
facilitatorNotes: The interrupted mouthful and congealing food give physical form to shock. Delaying the report makes readers observe the disruption before receiving its explanation.
evidence: The cabbage began to deposit a cold white grease on his plate.

questions.prompt: Which witnesses know the immediate event, and which supply an account of Mrs. Sinico’s life?
facilitatorNotes: Driver and porter describe the train event; husband and daughter describe habits and absence. Their evidence has different scope, and none reports her intention at that moment.
evidence: He was not in Dublin at the time of the accident

questions.prompt: Is No blame attached to anyone equivalent to a full explanation of the death?
facilitatorNotes: It closes an institutional inquiry into responsibility, particularly railway conduct. It neither reconstructs her inner life nor settles broader moral questions raised by the story.
evidence: No blame attached to anyone.

days.title: A Painful Case — part 3: the judgment turns
days.challenge: Follow changing self-judgments without accepting either as complete proof.
days.focus: Moral certainty, responsibility and loneliness.
days.context: Duffy has read the inquest report. His first response condemns Mrs. Sinico; his later walk alters the direction of that judgment.
days.contentNote: Grief, a death, guilt and severe isolation.

excerpt.locator: A Painful Case; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 32–38; opens “Mr. Duffy raised his eyes from the paper and gazed out of his window on the cheerless evening landsc”; closes “ing: the night was perfectly silent. He listened again: perfectly silent. He felt that he was alone.”.

questions.prompt: How does the claim that she degraded him expose a problem in his first response?
facilitatorNotes: He centers his own purity and reputation in her death. His disgust may protect him from recognizing her suffering or his limited knowledge of her later life.
evidence: Not merely had she degraded herself; she had degraded him.

questions.prompt: Does his later belief that he sentenced her to death establish direct causation?
facilitatorNotes: No. It records a reversal into guilt and recognition of rejected connection. Readers can discuss moral failure without assuming that one act fully caused a later death.
evidence: Why had he sentenced her to death?

questions.prompt: What changes between imagining her presence and the last repeated silence?
facilitatorNotes: Memory first seems tactile and audible; the final listening yields absence. The ending makes loneliness palpable while leaving uncertain whether insight will produce any change.
evidence: He listened again: perfectly silent. He felt that he was alone.

days.title: A Little Cloud — part 1: imagined authorship
days.challenge: Distinguish a character’s artistic ambition from what his attention actually selects.
days.focus: Self-fashioning and the glamour of elsewhere.
days.context: Little Chandler, a Dublin clerk, is about to meet Gallaher, an old acquaintance now working in London journalism.
days.contentNote: Class prejudice, drinking and references to adult nightlife.

excerpt.locator: A Little Cloud; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–39; opens “Eight years before he had seen his friend off at the North Wall and wished him godspeed. Gallaher ha”; closes “glasses, "and I've been to all the Bohemian cafés. Hot stuff! Not for a pious chap like you, Tommy."”.

questions.prompt: How does Chandler’s treatment of street children complicate his image of himself as a sensitive poet?
facilitatorNotes: He enjoys generalized melancholy but passes actual poverty without thought, using dehumanizing imagery. Sensitivity to an aesthetic scene does not guarantee attention to other people.
evidence: all that minute vermin-like life

questions.prompt: Why does he invent reviews and adjust his name before writing the poems?
facilitatorNotes: Recognition and a marketable Celtic identity occupy his imagination before the work itself. This does not disprove talent but reveals the gap between desired status and artistic practice.
evidence: He began to invent sentences and phrases from the notice which his book would get.

questions.prompt: What contrast between the men is conveyed by their whisky?
facilitatorNotes: Gallaher drinks boldly and neat; Chandler dilutes his and explains his modest habits. Their embodied performance rehearses the confidence and hesitation organizing the encounter.
evidence: Little Chandler allowed his whisky to be very much diluted.

days.title: A Little Cloud — part 2: competing performances
days.challenge: Read dialogue as a contest over status and value.
days.focus: The instability of admiration and contempt.
days.context: Chandler’s encounter with Gallaher has unsettled him. He admires his friend’s experience but begins to dislike the way Gallaher displays it.
days.contentNote: Drinking, sexual boasting and antisemitic/ethnic stereotypes voiced by characters; discuss their role in exposing those characters’ assumptions.

excerpt.locator: A Little Cloud; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 40–106; opens “Little Chandler said nothing until the barman returned with two glasses: then he touched his friend'”; closes “******”.

questions.prompt: Why does Chandler excuse Gallaher’s vulgarity even while noticing it?
facilitatorNotes: Gallaher embodies the worldly life Chandler envies, so dismissing him would threaten Chandler’s own dream. Admiration and distaste coexist rather than cleanly replace one another.
evidence: Little Chandler looked at his friend enviously.

questions.prompt: What makes the refused family invitation more than a scheduling disappointment to Chandler?
facilitatorNotes: He reads refusal as patronage and classifies Gallaher as inferior in birth and education. The injury becomes a struggle to assert worth and masculinity.
evidence: Gallaher was his inferior in birth and education.

questions.prompt: How does Gallaher’s projected marriage challenge his image of free adventure?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines marriage as a financial transaction, treating women and ethnic groups through prejudiced stereotypes. His freedom depends on acquiring somebody else’s wealth.
evidence: I mean to marry money.

days.title: A Little Cloud — part 3: the room at home
days.challenge: Compare a character’s resentful interpretation with narrated actions.
days.focus: Artistic longing, domestic labor and responsibility.
days.context: Back home after meeting Gallaher, Chandler holds his child while Annie goes to buy provisions he forgot. His imagined alternative life enters the room with him.
days.contentNote: A parent shouts at an infant; distress and remorse. The character’s racialized fantasy is presented for critical examination.

excerpt.locator: A Little Cloud; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 107–131; opens “Little Chandler sat in the room off the hall, holding a child in his arms. To save money they kept n”; closes “le the paroxysm of the child's sobbing grew less and less; and tears of remorse started to his eyes.”.

questions.prompt: What does the memory of buying the blouse reveal that Chandler’s cold reading of the photograph leaves out?
facilitatorNotes: The remembered episode contains his anxious care and Annie’s mixed but affectionate response. The photograph becomes a surface for his current resentment, not a complete account of their marriage.
evidence: He looked coldly into the eyes of the photograph and they answered coldly.

questions.prompt: How does reading Byron intensify the conflict between artistic feeling and immediate care?
facilitatorNotes: He wants to inhabit poetic melancholy but the child’s actual distress interrupts it. The clash tests whether he can respond to a person whose needs do not fit his desired mood.
evidence: The wailing of the child pierced the drum of his ear.

questions.prompt: How far does the last sentence resolve his earlier resentment?
facilitatorNotes: Remorse recognizes harm and fear, but the story gives no evidence of a lasting transformation. Stepping out of lamplight also returns him to withdrawal.
evidence: tears of remorse started to his eyes.

days.title: The Boarding House — part 1: a calculated intervention
days.challenge: Separate the narrator’s account, social conventions and a character’s strategic reasoning.
days.focus: Honor as protection and bargaining power.
days.context: Mrs. Mooney runs a boarding house. After allowing her daughter Polly’s relationship with a lodger to develop, she prepares to intervene.
days.contentNote: Domestic violence in the backstory and a sexual relationship interpreted through restrictive social conventions.

excerpt.locator: The Boarding House; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 1–11; opens “Mrs. Mooney was a butcher's daughter. She was a woman who was quite able to keep things to herself: ”; closes “fied her and she thought of some mothers she knew who could not get their daughters off their hands.”.

questions.prompt: How does the cleaver comparison connect Mrs. Mooney’s past to her approach to moral problems?
facilitatorNotes: Her history in a butcher’s business becomes a figure for decisive cutting through ambiguity. It suggests practical strength but also a potentially brutal simplification.
evidence: She dealt with moral problems as a cleaver deals with meat

questions.prompt: What is the force of the claim that there was no open complicity?
facilitatorNotes: The qualifier open preserves a tacit understanding while denying explicit agreement. Readers must distinguish inferred coordination from a stated plan.
evidence: There had been no open complicity between mother and daughter

questions.prompt: How does Mrs. Mooney’s account combine a real social inequality with a strategy for winning?
facilitatorNotes: She notes that a woman bears more reputational cost, yet calculates Doran’s job, savings and fear of publicity. Protection and self-interested bargaining are both present.
evidence: the girl has to bear the brunt.

days.title: The Boarding House — part 2: what is left offstage
days.challenge: Compare shifting viewpoints and an ending that withholds the decisive conversation.
days.focus: Coercion, agency and the limits of inferred agreement.
days.context: Mrs. Mooney has summoned Doran. The story now follows his anxiety, then Polly’s changing state as she waits.
days.contentNote: Sexual reputation, coercion, threats of violence and a character’s statement about self-harm.

excerpt.locator: The Boarding House; contiguous excerpt, source blocks 12–30; opens “Mr. Doran was very anxious indeed this Sunday morning. He had made two attempts to shave but his han”; closes “Then she remembered what she had been waiting for.”.

questions.prompt: How do Doran’s objections reveal both social pressure and his own prejudice?
facilitatorNotes: Fear for his job and public standing creates pressure; contempt for Polly’s grammar and family shows class prejudice. He also admits his participation, undermining a simple account of innocent entrapment.
evidence: Of course he had done it too.

questions.prompt: What does the staircase scene make physically visible about his apparent choice?
facilitatorNotes: He imagines upward escape but is pushed downward by social obligation and the threatening presence of Jack. Spatial movement turns abstract pressure into a staged descent.
evidence: a force pushed him downstairs step by step.

questions.prompt: Why end before readers hear Mrs. Mooney’s conversation with Doran?
facilitatorNotes: The omission makes us infer an arrangement from Polly’s summons and changing mood. It keeps the precise terms, Doran’s consent and Polly’s expectations from becoming settled facts.
evidence: Then she remembered what she had been waiting for.

days.title: Easter, 1916
days.challenge: Hold praise, personal dislike and political doubt together across a recurring refrain.
days.focus: Commemoration that refuses to become uncomplicated endorsement.
days.context: Yeats responds to the Irish Easter Rising and the deaths of its leaders. The speaker revisits people he once knew in ordinary social life; the poem itself does not supply a full history of the rising.
days.contentNote: Political violence, execution and mourning; the speaker also judges a woman’s political voice through gendered expectations.

excerpt.locator: Easter, 1916; complete individual work; opens “I have met them at close of day Coming with vivid faces From counter or desk among grey Eighteenth-c”; closes “ and in time to be, Wherever green is worn. Are changed, changed utterly: A terrible beauty is born.”.

questions.prompt: How does the repetition of polite meaningless words prepare for the refrain about change?
facilitatorNotes: Ordinary encounters initially seem trivial and theatrical; death retrospectively transforms their significance. The speaker’s earlier certainty becomes part of what must change.
evidence: Polite meaningless words,

questions.prompt: Is the stone an image of admirable steadfastness, dangerous rigidity, or both?
facilitatorNotes: A single purpose resists the living stream’s continual change. The later stone of the heart explicitly warns that sacrifice may harden feeling, while endurance remains impressive.
evidence:
Too long a sacrifice
Can make a stone of the heart.

questions.prompt: Why preserve the question about needless death even while writing the names into verse?
facilitatorNotes: Commemoration need not settle the political necessity of the sacrifice. The refrain’s terrible beauty binds admiration to cost, and naming acknowledges persons without erasing doubt.
evidence: Was it needless death after all?

days.title: Sixteen Dead Men
days.challenge: Track an imagined dialogue between living political calculation and the authority of the dead.
days.focus: The emotional consequences of execution for public argument.
days.context: The poem responds to executed Irish rebels during the First World War. Its addressed opponent proposes waiting until Germany is defeated; the speaker asks whether that reasoning can still command attention.
days.contentNote: Execution and the political afterlife of the dead.

excerpt.locator: Sixteen Dead Men; complete individual work; opens “O but we talked at large before The sixteen men were shot, But who can talk of give and take, What s”; closes “ have found Lord Edward and Wolfe Tone, Or meddle with our give and take That converse bone to bone.”.

questions.prompt: How does the boiling pot change the force of the opening talk of give and take?
facilitatorNotes: Negotiation sounds measured, while the dead are imagined as continuing to intensify public feeling. The image makes execution an active political force after bodily death.
evidence: To stir the boiling pot.

questions.prompt: Why oppose logic to a bony thumb rather than to another argument?
facilitatorNotes: The bodily remnant makes sacrifice resistant to ordinary debate. It can suggest the power of memory and the danger that emotionally authoritative symbols displace reasoning.
evidence: MacDonagh’s bony thumb?

questions.prompt: What does the final conversation bone to bone imply about the audience for compromise?
facilitatorNotes: The dead are imagined joining earlier rebels in a historical community beyond current bargaining. The living speaker cannot simply negotiate with that symbolic conversation.
evidence: That converse bone to bone.

days.title: The Rose Tree
days.challenge: Evaluate a symbolic argument whose apparent necessity depends on its premises.
days.focus: The rhetoric of sacrificial violence.
days.context: Yeats stages an imagined exchange between Pearse and Connolly. This is a lyric dialogue, not a transcript of their words.
days.contentNote: An imagined argument for political blood sacrifice; examine its rhetoric rather than treating it as an instruction.

excerpt.locator: The Rose Tree; complete individual work; opens ““O words are lightly spoken” Said Pearse to Connolly, “Maybe a breath of politic words Has withered ”; closes “hed away? O plain as plain can be There’s nothing but our own red blood Can make a right Rose Tree.””.

questions.prompt: What possible causes of the rose tree’s decline are offered before the proposed remedy?
facilitatorNotes: Empty political language and a hostile wind from across the sea offer internal and external explanations. Maybe marks uncertainty that the ending later suppresses.
evidence: Maybe a breath of politic words

questions.prompt: What does Connolly’s gardening language promise?
facilitatorNotes: Water would restore green growth, bloom and communal pride. The natural cycle makes restoration appear both desirable and potentially simple.
evidence: To make the green come out again

questions.prompt: Which unproved premise makes blood appear to be the only remaining answer?
facilitatorNotes: All wells are said to be dry, eliminating ordinary water. Plain as plain claims obviousness, but the metaphor does not demonstrate that political alternatives are exhausted or sacrifice effective.
evidence: When all the wells are parched away?

days.title: On a Political Prisoner
days.challenge: Distinguish reported action, rhetorical questioning and idealized memory.
days.focus: Who controls the meaning of a woman’s political transformation.
days.context: A speaker imagines an imprisoned woman’s patience with a gull and recalls her earlier outdoor life. Notice how much of the account is supplied by the observer.
days.contentNote: Political imprisonment and a speaker’s hostile judgment of political activism.

excerpt.locator: On a Political Prisoner; complete individual work; opens “She that but little patience knew, From childhood on, had now so much A grey gull lost its fear and ”; closes “ stare Upon the cloudy canopy, While under its storm-beaten breast Cried out the hollows of the sea.”.

questions.prompt: What specific behavior supports the claim that imprisonment has changed her patience?
facilitatorNotes: The gull loses fear, tolerates touch and feeds from her fingers. These actions imply sustained quiet attention, although the poem supplies no access to her own explanation.
evidence: A grey gull lost its fear and flew

questions.prompt: Does the question beginning Did she establish what the prisoner remembered?
facilitatorNotes: No. It projects the speaker’s preferred contrast between youthful beauty and abstract political enmity. The question form exposes the distance between speculation and testimony.
evidence: Did she in touching that lone wing

questions.prompt: How does the final bird comparison complicate the opening captive scene?
facilitatorNotes: The remembered rider becomes a bird at the edge of flight over a turbulent sea; the prison gull links captivity with an image of freedom. Readers can find admiration while also questioning the speaker’s idealization.
evidence: Like any rock-bred, sea-borne bird:

days.title: The Leaders of the Crowd
days.challenge: Follow an argument that turns critically upon its own preferred alternative.
days.focus: Accusation, solitary inquiry and the attractions of collective life.
days.context: Helicon invokes the traditional mountain of poetic inspiration. The poem opposes rumor to scholarship, then complicates that opposition in its final lines.

excerpt.locator: The Leaders of the Crowd; complete individual work; opens “They must to keep their certainty accuse All that are different of a base intent; Pull down establis”; closes “y come. They have loud music, hope every day renewed And heartier loves; that lamp is from the tomb.”.

questions.prompt: Why does the opening make accusation necessary to the leaders’ certainty?
facilitatorNotes: They preserve certainty by assigning base motives to difference, insulating belief from challenge. The poem locates a psychological function behind public denunciation.
evidence: They must to keep their certainty accuse

questions.prompt: How does the gutter/Helicon comparison attack both information and art?
facilitatorNotes: Rumor is treated as news and slander as song; degraded material is falsely elevated into cultural authority. The contrast tests the sources that support public conviction.
evidence: Or calumny a song.

questions.prompt: Why does the lamp from the tomb prevent an easy victory for the solitary student?
facilitatorNotes: The crowd retains music, renewed hope and warmer love, while scholarship’s lamp is associated with death. The ending gives the rejected side human attractions and questions the cost of withdrawal.
evidence: And heartier loves; that lamp is from the tomb.

days.title: The Second Coming
days.challenge: Track how a confident announcement becomes a disturbing, unfinished question.
days.focus: Historical crisis and the instability of prophetic interpretation.
days.context: The poem uses Christian expectations of a second coming but gives the speaker a radically different vision. Spiritus Mundi names a world-spirit or shared store of images within the poem’s imaginative system.
days.contentNote: Apocalyptic violence and imagery of cultural collapse.

excerpt.locator: The Second Coming; complete individual work; opens “Turning and turning in the widening gyre The falcon cannot hear the falconer; Things fall apart; the”; closes “ng cradle, And what rough beast, its hour come round at last, Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?”.

questions.prompt: What relation breaks in the falcon image, and how does it prepare the widening political claims?
facilitatorNotes: The creature can no longer hear its guiding human voice. Expanding circular motion represents a loss of communication and control before the poem asserts general disorder.
evidence: The falcon cannot hear the falconer;

questions.prompt: How does the repeated Surely expose the speaker’s effort to make sense of disorder?
facilitatorNotes: The repetition sounds assured but insists on an interpretation not yet seen. The image that follows troubles rather than confirms the expected Christian revelation.
evidence: Surely some revelation is at hand;

questions.prompt: Why end with a question about birth instead of an account of arrival?
facilitatorNotes: The beast is approaching an ominous future whose meaning remains unresolved. Bethlehem and the cradle invert a familiar salvation story; the question withholds a stable final prophecy.
evidence: Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?

days.title: A Prayer for My Daughter
days.challenge: Evaluate a protective prayer that also prescribes another person’s life.
days.focus: Care, gender, custom and the wish for inward freedom.
days.context: A father hears a storm while his child sleeps. His hopes range from kindness and friendship to restrictions on beauty, opinion and place.
days.contentNote: Gendered expectations and mythological judgments about women are part of the speaker’s argument, open to criticism.

excerpt.locator: A Prayer for My Daughter; complete individual work; opens “Once more the storm is howling and half hid Under this cradle-hood and coverlid My child sleeps on. ”; closes “ence and beauty born? Ceremony’s a name for the rich horn. And custom for the spreading laurel tree.”.

questions.prompt: How does the storm operate as both physical event and imagined history?
facilitatorNotes: Wind threatens roof and landscape, while the speaker imagines future years dancing violently. The cradle makes broad historical fear immediate and domestic.
evidence: Out of the murderous innocence of the sea.

questions.prompt: What is appealing and what is restrictive in the wish that the daughter become a hidden tree?
facilitatorNotes: Rootedness, generous song and resilience promise security; hidden and one perpetual place also limit mobility and public life. Both readings should use the image’s actual terms.
evidence: May she become a flourishing hidden tree

questions.prompt: Does rejecting hatred necessarily justify rejecting opinions?
facilitatorNotes: The poem moves from a persuasive warning about hatred to a much broader prescription against opinion. Readers may challenge that inference while recognizing the speaker’s personal disappointments and desire to protect.
evidence: So let her think opinions are accursed.

days.title: Demon and Beast
days.challenge: Follow a temporary experience while testing the speaker’s later explanation of it.
days.focus: Freedom from desire and the paradox of mastery.
days.context: The speaker experiences a brief release from hatred and desire. Gallery portraits, ordinary birds and ascetic figures become stages in his attempt to understand it.
days.contentNote: Religious asceticism and self-denial are invoked as historical images, not practical advice.

excerpt.locator: Demon and Beast; complete individual work; opens “For certain minutes at the least That crafty demon and that loud beast That plague me day and night ”; closes “ more Starved upon the shore And withered to a bag of bones: What had the Caesars but their thrones?”.

questions.prompt: What changes in the portraits when the demon and beast disappear?
facilitatorNotes: Formerly distant or contentious figures seem companionable because he can regard others’ thoughts as dear. The change is in his mode of attention, not in the paintings themselves.
evidence: For all men’s thoughts grew clear

questions.prompt: Why does the ordinary bird’s power matter beside the elevated gallery scene?
facilitatorNotes: An absurd, happy creature can move his whole nature without ambition or ideological agreement. The shift makes unguarded attention to ordinary life the test of his release.
evidence:
A stupid happy creature
Could rouse my whole nature.

questions.prompt: How does wanting to prolong freedom complicate the claim of freedom from desire?
facilitatorNotes: He desires the desireless state and suspects aging rather than chosen mastery caused it. The final ascetics suggest another possibility, but their bodily cost complicates triumph.
evidence: To make it linger half a day.

days.title: Towards Break of Day
days.challenge: Distinguish physical touch, memory and the uncertain sharing of dreams.
days.focus: Intimacy that cannot erase separate inward worlds.
days.context: Two sleepers approach waking. The speaker recalls a beloved waterfall and wonders whether the woman beside him has dreamed the same dream.

excerpt.locator: Towards Break of Day; complete individual work; opens “Was it the double of my dream The woman that by me lay Dreamed, or did we halve a dream Under the fi”; closes “terer sleep The marvellous stag of Arthur, That lofty white stag, leap From mountain steep to steep.”.

questions.prompt: How does the speaker explain the waterfall’s incomparable value?
facilitatorNotes: Repeated memory enlarges childhood delight. Its value exceeds the physical object, which helps explain why touching stone and water would not recover the whole experience.
evidence:
My memories had magnified
So many times childish delight.

questions.prompt: Why accuse heaven over the limit of touch?
facilitatorNotes: The speaker experiences a mismatch between material contact and the immaterial intensity of love. The accusation turns disappointment into a proposed law of existence, which readers can question.
evidence:
Nothing that we love over-much
Is ponderable to our touch.

questions.prompt: Does the woman’s final dream answer the opening question?
facilitatorNotes: It provides a different image—the elusive white stag—and calls her sleep bitterer, suggesting analogous longing without identical experience. The relation remains partly inaccessible.
evidence: The marvellous stag of Arthur,

days.title: To Be Carved on a Stone at Ballylee
days.challenge: Develop a sustained reading of a six-line inscription through diction, form and future tense.
days.focus: Material restoration and the hoped-for survival of a name.
days.context: Read slowly several times, attending to the three rhymed pairs. The poem imagines its own words carved into the restored building.

excerpt.locator: To Be Carved on a Stone at Ballylee; complete individual work; opens “I, the poet William Yeats, With old mill boards and sea-green slates, And smithy work from the Gort ”; closes “Restored this tower for my wife George; And may these characters remain When all is ruin once again.”.

questions.prompt: Why name old boards, local slates and forge work in a monument to a poet?
facilitatorNotes: The list grounds poetic self-commemoration in reused materials and communal craft. It records how the tower was restored instead of only praising its owner.
evidence: With old mill boards and sea-green slates,

questions.prompt: How do the opening self-identification and the gift to George distribute credit and purpose?
facilitatorNotes: The I foregrounds the poet’s authorship, but the restoration is for his wife and relies on named materials and labor. Discuss both self-inscription and domestic dedication.
evidence: Restored this tower for my wife George;

questions.prompt: What does once again do to the apparent permanence of a carved inscription?
facilitatorNotes: It places restoration within a cycle that includes renewed ruin. The may is a wish, not certainty: even durable words are asked to outlast the building’s present order.
evidence: When all is ruin once again.

days.title: The good-morrow
days.challenge: Reconstruct an argument that moves from awakening through geography to an impossible-sounding conclusion.
days.focus: Mutual love as an alternative scale of value.
days.context: The speaker addresses a lover at waking. Early modern spelling is retained; read the syntax before interpreting the geographical conceits.

excerpt.locator: The good-morrow.; complete individual work; opens “I WONDER by my troth, what thou, and I Did, till we lov'd? were we not wean'd till then? But suck'd ”; closes “equally; If our two loves be one, or, thou and I Love so alike, that none doe slacken, none can die.”.

questions.prompt: What does the opening claim about infancy and sleep do to earlier pleasures?
facilitatorNotes: It retrospectively demotes them to preparation or dreams. This is the speaker’s totalizing claim for present love, not a neutral biography.
evidence: were we not wean'd till then?

questions.prompt: How can one room become everywhere without either lover traveling?
facilitatorNotes: Mutual attention gives the room the experiential completeness claimed for discovered worlds. The comparison competes with exploration while borrowing its language of possession.
evidence: And makes one little roome, an every where.

questions.prompt: What condition governs the promise that their love cannot die?
facilitatorNotes: The conclusion depends on equal mixture or equal love with no slackening. The conditional if leaves a vulnerability inside the confident promise.
evidence: If our two loves be one, or, thou and I

days.title: The Sunne Rising
days.challenge: Follow a speaker who changes tactics while pretending to command the cosmos.
days.focus: Hyperbole, intimacy and the appropriation of public power.
days.context: The lovers are interrupted by sunlight. The speaker first scolds the sun, then gives it a new job.
days.contentNote: An intimate bedroom address uses imperial and gendered assumptions as part of its extravagant rhetoric.

excerpt.locator: The Sunne Rising.; complete individual work; opens “BUSIE old foole, unruly Sunne, Why dost thou thus, Through windowes, and through curtaines call on u”; closes “ng us. Shine here to us, and thou art every where; This bed thy center is, these walls, thy spheare.”.

questions.prompt: How do schoolboys, apprentices and courtiers help define love’s imagined exemption?
facilitatorNotes: They belong to schedules and hierarchical duties; the speaker claims love lies beyond those measures. The scolding voice itself imitates an authority he rejects.
evidence: Nor houres, dayes, moneths, which are the rags of time.

questions.prompt: Why does the proposed wink fail as a demonstration of power over the sun?
facilitatorNotes: He can shut out its light but would also lose sight of the beloved. The boast exposes dependence and lets desire defeat the claimed mastery.
evidence: But that I would not lose her sight so long:

questions.prompt: Does the last stanza dismiss political hierarchy or reproduce it within the room?
facilitatorNotes: It dismisses external princes as imitations while assigning the woman states and the man princely power. The intimate world borrows the unequal structure it claims to surpass.
evidence: She'is all States, and all Princes, I,

days.title: The Canonization
days.challenge: Trace a defense that turns its accusers’ terms into an imagined future authority.
days.focus: The making of lovers into saints through poetry.
days.context: Canonization means recognition as a saint. The speaker applies religious and memorial language to an intimate relationship under criticism.
days.contentNote: Religious language is used provocatively to describe romantic and sexual union.

excerpt.locator: The Canonization.; complete individual work; opens “FOR Godsake hold your tongue, and let me love, Or chide my palsie, or my gout, My five gray haires, ”; closes “t they did all to you epitomize,) Countries, Townes, Courts: Beg from above A patterne of your love!”.

questions.prompt: How does the second stanza expose the absurdity of conventional love hyperbole?
facilitatorNotes: It asks whether sighs literally sink ships or tears flood property. By denying public harm, the speaker asks the critic to leave private love alone.
evidence: What merchants ships have my sighs drown'd?

questions.prompt: How do the phoenix and the two sexes challenge ordinary separation?
facilitatorNotes: The pair becomes one creature that dies and rises, making difference and union coexist. The poem calls this mysterious rather than explaining it through ordinary physical identity.
evidence: The Phœnix ridle hath more wit

questions.prompt: Why are sonnet rooms and an urn alternatives to chronicles and large tombs?
facilitatorNotes: Careful poetic form can preserve significance without public power or expensive scale. The poem performs the memorial it predicts and imagines later readers petitioning the lovers.
evidence: We'll build in sonnets pretty roomes;

days.title: Aire and Angels
days.challenge: Test a changing analogy whose conclusion introduces a new inequality.
days.focus: Embodied love and the limits of a supposedly spiritual argument.
days.context: The speaker moves among angels, bodies and an overloaded boat to explain where love can reside.
days.contentNote: The final comparison asserts a gender hierarchy that the discussion explicitly examines.

excerpt.locator: Aire and Angels.; complete individual work; opens “TWICE or thrice had I loved thee, Before I knew thy face or name; So in a voice, so in a shapelesse ”; closes “st such disparitie As is twixt Aire and Angells puritie, 'Twixt womens love, and mens will ever bee.”.

questions.prompt: What problem does the first stanza identify in a wholly bodiless love?
facilitatorNotes: The soul needs limbs to act, so love likewise needs an embodied form. Lovely glorious nothing acknowledges attraction while questioning its capacity to become a relation.
evidence: Love must not be, but take a body too,

questions.prompt: Why does the boat require ballast and then become overburdened?
facilitatorNotes: Physical particularity should stabilize love, but fascination with every feature overwhelms it. The revision seeks an intermediate relation between abstraction and sheer sensory abundance.
evidence: I saw, I had loves pinnace overfraught,

questions.prompt: Does the final hierarchy between men’s and women’s love follow necessarily from the earlier need for embodiment?
facilitatorNotes: No; the angel/air analogy supplies a gendered assignment whose superiority is asserted. Students may explain the historical conceit while challenging the inference.
evidence: 'Twixt womens love, and mens will ever bee.

days.title: A Valediction: of weeping
days.challenge: Track tears through three distinct systems of comparison without treating them as literal events.
days.focus: Parting, reflected identity and emotional pressure.
days.context: A valediction is a farewell. The speaker transforms tears successively into coins, globes and threatening seas.

excerpt.locator: A Valediction: of weeping.; complete individual work; opens “LET me powre forth My teares before thy face, whil'st I stay here, For thy face coines them, and thy”; closes “ thou and I sigh one anothers breath, Who e'r sighes most, is cruellest, and hasts the others death.”.

questions.prompt: How does the beloved’s reflected face give the tears value?
facilitatorNotes: Like a stamped coin, a tear becomes precious by carrying her image. The image ties the speaker’s grief to recognition and the fear of losing her presence.
evidence: For thy face coines them, and thy stampe they beare,

questions.prompt: How does the globe comparison enlarge the stakes of a single falling tear?
facilitatorNotes: An image turns a small round surface into a world; mixed tears then threaten to dissolve that world. Scale magnifies emotional loss while exposing the conceit’s imaginative extravagance.
evidence: A globe, yea world by that impression grow,

questions.prompt: What change in the speaker’s attitude toward tears occurs by the final stanza?
facilitatorNotes: He begins asking permission to weep and ends asking the beloved to stop, linking her grief to danger. The supposed shared breath can sound intimate or emotionally coercive.
evidence: Who e'r sighes most, is cruellest, and hasts the others death.

days.title: The broken heart
days.challenge: Follow an argument whose successive comparisons change what survival means.
days.focus: The difference between continuing to feel and being able to love again.
days.context: The speaker rejects the idea that love simply lasts through ordinary time, then explains the fragmentary condition of his heart.
days.contentNote: Violent and disease imagery expresses emotional injury.

excerpt.locator: The broken heart.; complete individual work; opens “HE is starke mad, who ever sayes, That he hath beene in love an houre, Yet not that love so soone de”; closes “r faces, so My ragges of heart can like, wish, and adore, But after one such love, can love no more.”.

questions.prompt: Why does saying love cannot last an hour not mean it is too brief or weak?
facilitatorNotes: Love is presented as so destructive that it can consume many hearts within that time. Plague and burning powder measure intensity rather than mere duration.
evidence: But that it can tenne in lesse space devour;

questions.prompt: How does the third stanza reject the usual idea that a lover gives away a heart?
facilitatorNotes: If the beloved possessed it, it would supposedly teach pity; because pity is absent, the speaker argues love shattered it instead. This is an emotionally interested inference, not proof about her inner life.
evidence: Mine would have taught thine heart to show

questions.prompt: What can the surviving fragments do that the whole heart once did differently?
facilitatorNotes: They can like, wish and adore but supposedly cannot unite in another total love. The mirror simile lets persistence coexist with damage and divided attention.
evidence: My ragges of heart can like, wish, and adore,

days.title: A Valediction: forbidding mourning
days.challenge: Compare successive analogies and notice how a conditional revises apparent certainty.
days.focus: A claim for continuity through physical separation.
days.context: The speaker asks for a quiet farewell, distinguishing their love from kinds dependent on immediate sensory presence.

excerpt.locator: A Valediction: forbidding mourning.; complete individual work; opens “AS virtuous men passe mildly away, And whisper to their soules, to goe, Whilst some of their sad fri”; closes “th'other foot, obliquely runne; Thy firmnes makes my circle just, And makes me end, where I begunne.”.

questions.prompt: Why compare the farewell to the quiet death of virtuous people?
facilitatorNotes: The analogy values inward assurance over visible display. It may console, but also asks the listener to accept the speaker’s authority over how grief should be expressed.
evidence: So let us melt, and make no noise,

questions.prompt: How does beaten gold change separation from a breach into expansion?
facilitatorNotes: A continuous substance spreads thinner without breaking. It makes distance a change in form rather than loss of unity, though it remains a chosen image rather than a guarantee.
evidence: Like gold to ayery thinnesse beate.

questions.prompt: What does the fixed compass foot actually do, and why does that matter?
facilitatorNotes: It leans and responds as the other travels, so fixed does not mean inert. The eventual circle requires both partners; discuss whether the assigned roles remain unequal despite reciprocity.
evidence: It leanes, and hearkens after it,

days.title: The Extasie
days.challenge: Sustain attention through a long philosophical poem that argues back toward the body.
days.focus: Why spiritual intimacy still needs material expression.
days.context: Two lovers remain still and silent while the poem imagines their souls negotiating. The spelling extasie suggests a standing outside oneself.
days.contentNote: Philosophical discussion of romantic and bodily intimacy.

excerpt.locator: The Extasie.; complete individual work; opens “WHERE, like a pillow on a bed, A Pregnant banke swel'd up, to rest The violets reclining head, Sat w”; closes “this dialogue of one, Let him still marke us, he shall see Small change, when we'are to bodies gone.”.

questions.prompt: How do bodily details at the start complicate the claim that this experience is purely spiritual?
facilitatorNotes: Hands, eye-beams, the swelling bank and violets make sensory contact foundational. The souls’ departure depends on a scene of embodied intimacy.
evidence: Our hands were firmely cimented

questions.prompt: What does the transplanted violet explain about the lovers’ supposed new soul?
facilitatorNotes: Transplanting strengthens and enlarges the living plant; their union similarly transforms existing mixtures. The analogy suggests mutual enhancement rather than the simple erasure of two identities.
evidence: A single violet transplant,

questions.prompt: Why does the poem finally call the body a book rather than dross?
facilitatorNotes: Embodiment communicates inward love to the lovers and witnesses. Calling it alloy also grants an enabling function; the ending argues that spirit needs expression rather than despising matter.
evidence: But yet the body is his booke.

days.title: A Lecture upon the Shadow
days.challenge: Test the fit and limits of a natural process used as an argument about love.
days.focus: Disclosure, self-deception and a demand for permanence.
days.context: A speaker turns a walk near noon into a lesson addressed to a lover. Sunlight supplies the poem’s model and its central difficulty.

excerpt.locator: A Lecture upon the Shadow.; complete individual work; opens “STAND still, and I will read to thee A Lecture, Love, in loves philosophy. These three houres that w”; closes “Love is a growing, or full constant light; And his first minute, after noone, is night.”.

questions.prompt: What do the morning shadows correspond to in the early relationship?
facilitatorNotes: Disguises and concern about other observers; the couple itself produces them. The noon image imagines clarity achieved by standing over those earlier shadows.
evidence: Disguises did, and shadowes, flow,

questions.prompt: How do the later shadows differ from the earlier ones?
facilitatorNotes: The earlier disguises blind outsiders; later ones would blind the lovers themselves. Decline therefore changes secrecy from mutual protection into mutual deception.
evidence: Will worke upon our selves, and blind our eyes.

questions.prompt: What tension does the wish to remain at noon introduce into the lecture’s natural analogy?
